newsitem.title: USA: Bankers cheer imminent closing of Peru Brady deal.
newsitem.headline: Bankers cheer imminent closing of Peru Brady deal.

text.p: Peru is expected to close its long-awaited Brady plan with commercial bank creditors Friday in New York and bankers close to the deal were ecstatic that the agreement was on the verge of being finalized.

"We are very pleased. We expect it to close tomorrow. It has been a long time since the 1983 agreement that we had any formal contract that Peru has lived up to and I think it is a positive sign for them. It shows that normalcy can return despite their political issues with the hostages," said one banking source close to the deal who requested anonymity.
A spokesman for Citicorp's Citibank, which chairs the bank advisory committee, confirmed that the Brady agreement with Peru would close on Friday.
The total amount of Peruvian foreign debt, including principal and interest, to be restructured under the Brady agreement is estimated at around $8.0 billion.
Earlier, the Peruvian government said in Quito that the country's Economy Minister Jorge Camet was travelling to New York on Thursday for the official closing of the Brady accord.
"This is a good sign for Peru. They are the last of the Latins to do a Brady deal. It's about time," said the source.
Emerging market debt experts cited several reasons for delays in the Brady closing but also gave a sigh of relief that the closing would be completed Friday.
"It is just a big relief. It's finally coming to an end," said Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at BankBoston Corp.

One market expert said a major reason for the delays was the reconciliation process on the Peruvian loans, which was extremely complicated because the loans were very actively traded in the marketplace.
Emerging market debt experts said the closing of the Brady deal would be a positive step because it would open the way for Peru to tap the international capital markets.

"Even though they don't need the money, the natural progression of things would be for them to tap the market in order to create a benchmark," said Marco Santamaria, vice president of fixed income research at ING Barings in New York.
"I think Peru will enter the markets fairly soon with an inaugural issue to establish a benchmark," added another emerging market expert.
Peru, which is not yet rated by Standard and Poor's Corp, received a B2 sovereign rating for its foreign currency issue last year by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
